content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidelines in July 2020 to prevent the transmission of hepatitis B virus (HBV) from mother to child. These guidelines emphasize the use of antiviral prophylaxis during pregnancy to reduce the risk of HBV transmission. The document also outlines a framework for verifying global control of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) prevalence in children by 2020. The WHO estimates that in 2015, approximately 257 million people worldwide were living with chronic HBV infection. The prevalence of HBV is higher in regions with low birth dose vaccination coverage, such as Africa, where timely birth dose (TBD) coverage was only 10% in 2017. To address this, WHO recommends universal immunization with the hepatitis B vaccine (HepB) as part of national immunization programs. The first dose should ideally be administered within 24 hours of birth. By 2018, 189 countries had introduced HepB for infants, achieving a global coverage of 84% for the three-dose series. WHO has set ambitious goals to eliminate hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030, aiming for a 90% reduction in incidence and a 65% reduction in mortality. For HBV, the target includes achieving less than 1% prevalence of chronic HBV infection in children under five years of age by 2020. This requires additional interventions, such as preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) through antenatal testing for HBsAg, administration of hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG), and peripartum antiviral prophylaxis. The guidelines also highlight the importance of regional and global efforts to harmonize verification frameworks for achieving the <1% prevalence target. Verification involves assessing HBsAg prevalence in children through serological surveys and ensuring high and sustained HepB vaccination coverage. WHO provides technical guidance to support countries in conducting nationally representative surveys to evaluate the impact of their immunization programs. To verify progress, countries must demonstrate low HBsAg prevalence among vaccinated cohorts of children and provide evidence of high HepB vaccination coverage at national and subnational levels. Additional data, such as antenatal HBV testing coverage, availability of HBIG, and post-vaccination serological testing (PVST), may also be required. Verification panels, appointed by WHO regional directors, review submitted data and assess whether countries have met the established targets. The guidelines emphasize the need for sustained efforts to maintain verification status, including regular monitoring of vaccination coverage and disease prevalence. WHO encourages countries to integrate TBD into their national immunization schedules and to implement policies for antenatal HBV testing and prevention of perinatal transmission.
